title: Time-Series Forecasting using Continuous Variables-Based Quantum Neural Networks
journal_or_venue: 2024 16th International Conference on COMmunication Systems & NETworkS (COMSNETS)
abstract_summary: The paper evaluates continuous-variable quantum neural networks (CVQNNs) for time-series forecasting on simulated real-world datasets (energy consumption and stock prices), comparing performance to a discrete-variable variational quantum linear solver (VQLS) and classical neural networks. Results on simulators show CVQNNs naturally handle continuous data and controlled nonlinearity with fewer parameters, and that multi-step CVQNN forecasting can outperform iterative one-step prediction in some cases.
methodology_description: The authors implement and evaluate continuous-variable quantum neural networks (CVQNNs) for time-series forecasting and compare them against a variational quantum linear solver (VQLS) and classical neural networks. They encode continuous input features (previous time-series values) directly into qumodes using displacement gates, build layers composed of interferometers (U1, U2), squeezing (S), displacements (D) and one-mode non-Gaussian gates (Φ) to realize affine + nonlinear transforms, and read out position expectation values <x> per mode as continuous outputs. Training is performed in a hybrid variational fashion: circuit parameters are initialised randomly and optimised by a classical optimizer (ADAM via the TensorFlow backend in Strawberry Fields) to minimise a mean-squared-error loss (MSE). For multi-step forecasting a weighted MSE with a diagonal weight matrix (weights summing to 1) is used. As a benchmark, a VQLS implementation (Qiskit) is used to obtain OLS-type regression solutions via variational optimisation; Hadamard-test circuitry is used to form the VQLS cost. Experiments are run on simulators (Strawberry Fields TensorFlow backend for CVQNNs and Qiskit statevector simulator for VQLS). Performance comparisons include classical matrix inversion and a classical neural network with the same number of trainable parameters. The methodology explores architecture depth (1–3 CVQNN layers) and both one-step (iterative) and block/multi-step forecasting (four-step) strategies, reporting MSE/absolute error metrics on real-world datasets.
experimental_setup: All quantum experiments were performed on simulators: CVQNNs were implemented and trained using Strawberry Fields with the TensorFlow backend (analytical expectation-value evaluation) and VQLS benchmarks were executed using Qiskit's statevector simulator. No physical QPU was used. Data were scaled to limit displacement magnitudes (to respect Fock-space truncation) and split 4:1 into train and test sets. Model variants used 4 qumodes (input features), and CVQNN depths of 1–3 layers; multi-step forecasts predicted blocks of 4 future timesteps.
dataset_used: Financial datasets: IBM average stock price time series (≈80 instances) and Yahoo average stock price time series (≈100 instances). Additionally, a non-financial industrial Energy Consumption dataset (office space) with ≈200 instances was used. Sources cited: Macrotrends (IBM), Kaggle (Yahoo dataset), and a referenced energy dataset.

key_findings: [supported] Continuous-variable quantum neural networks (CVQNNs) can directly encode continuous-valued time-series inputs via displacement gates and produce continuous-valued outputs by measuring mode quadrature expectations.

[supported] CVQNN layers implement both affine (linear) and non-linear transformations analogous to classical neural-network layers (interferometers, squeezers, displacements, and non-Gaussian gates), and the non-linearities are parameterized and trainable.

[supported] On small, simulated datasets (IBM stock, Yahoo stock, office Energy Consumption), CVQNNs achieved forecasting performance comparable to or better than baseline methods (classical NN and a DV variational quantum linear solver (VQLS)) in some cases; e.g., lower test error on the IBM stock dataset compared to a classical NN with the same number of trainable parameters.
[supported] Increasing the number of CVQNN layers improved optimization behavior (made it easier to find lower minima), mirroring behavior known from classical deep networks.

[supported] Multi-step (block) forecasting implemented natively in CVQNNs performed better (less error accumulation) than iteratively applying one-step forecasts on predicted data (point-wise iterative prediction) in the experiments reported (e.g., Yahoo dataset).
[supported] Practical simulation constraints require scaling inputs before encoding to avoid populating Fock states beyond the simulator's truncation cutoff.

[supported] The authors did not demonstrate any runtime speed-up or provable quantum advantage; simulations were run on classical hardware and the study did not measure hardware speed/performance advantages.

[supported] Extending VQLS (a DV variational solver) to directly produce multiple continuous-valued outputs for block multi-step forecasting is not straightforward in the manner CVQNNs provide, making CVQNNs more naturally suited for block prediction tasks in the reported work.

[speculative] CVQNNs (and CV-based QML generally) 'promise' performance advantages over discrete-variable QML for tasks involving continuous data and controlled non-linearity, but this is presented as an expectation and not demonstrated experimentally on hardware or at scale in this work.

[speculative] CVQNN circuits are shallow and parameterized, making them suitable for near-term (NISQ) photonic/continuous-variable devices — this claim is forward-looking and not validated on physical quantum hardware in this paper.
results_summary: The paper implements and evaluates continuous-variable quantum neural networks (CVQNNs) on simulated photonic quantum circuits for time-series forecasting (one-step and multi-step) using small real-world datasets (IBM and Yahoo stock prices, and office energy consumption). Empirically, CVQNNs can natively encode continuous inputs, produce continuous outputs, and learn affine plus parameterized non-linear transformations. In simulations, CVQNNs achieved comparable forecasting accuracy to classical neural nets and a DV variational linear solver (VQLS), with notable advantages in multi-step (block) forecasting where CVQNNs reduced error accumulation versus iterated one-step prediction. Increasing network depth improved optimization behavior. The study was limited to classical simulation (Fock-space truncation constraints) and did not claim or demonstrate a runtime quantum advantage.

quantum_advantage_detail: The paper does not claim or demonstrate a provable or empirical quantum runtime advantage. Experiments were performed on classical simulators with small datasets; the authors explicitly note simulation scaling limits and state that it is impossible to experimentally measure speed-ups in this study. Claims about potential benefits of CV representations over DV are presented as expectations or motivations rather than demonstrated advantages.
limitations: Experiments were performed on small datasets (80–200 instances), limiting generalizability to larger, real-world financial time series.
All experiments were run on simulators (classical simulation of quantum circuits); exponential scaling and limited classical resources make it difficult to handle larger amounts of data.
Because simulations used a truncated Fock space, the authors had to scale input data to avoid large displacements, introducing an approximation and potential bias from the cutoff dimension.
It was not possible to experimentally measure or demonstrate runtime advantages or quantum speed-ups due to simulation-only evaluation.
The CVQNN implementations used a small number of qumodes/neuron-equivalents (four), which constrains expressivity in the reported experiments.
Iterative one-step forecasting accumulated error over multiple steps (poor performance when iterating one-step predictions), indicating limitations of naive iterative forecasting.

Optimization behavior depended on circuit depth: shallow (one-layer) CVQNNs failed to reach good minima, requiring additional layers to obtain comparable errors—indicating sensitivity to architecture/depth.
The work is confined to fully quantum architectures (no classical NN layers), so hybrid approaches were intentionally not evaluated in these experiments.
[inferred] The results do not include noise or hardware error models; therefore the impact of realistic device noise on CVQNN performance is unknown.
[inferred] No empirical or theoretical evidence of asymptotic or provable advantage over classical methods was demonstrated; scaling/complexity advantages remain unproven.
[inferred] Hyperparameter sensitivity (e.g., learning rate, batch size, Fock cutoff) and robustness were not extensively explored and may affect reproducibility and performance.
[inferred] Data scaling required by the Fock-space truncation could distort the natural data distributions and may affect applicability to financial datasets with wide dynamic ranges.

key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — Continuous-variable quantum neural networks (CVQNNs) are reported to outperform matched-size classical neural networks on several small financial time-series forecasting tasks (example: IBM stock averaged test MSE ~0.06 vs classical NN ~0.424).
#idea:quantum-advantage — Multi-step (block) CVQNN forecasting can outperform iterative one-step prediction in some experiments (improved MSE on Yahoo multi-step example: 4.23e-07 reported).

#idea:hybrid-approach — Training performed in a hybrid variational fashion: quantum circuit parameters optimized by classical optimizers (ADAM via TensorFlow backend), demonstrating a practical hybrid QPU-CPU workflow (simulated here).

#idea:near-term-feasibility — CVQNNs naturally accept continuous inputs via displacement gates (qumodes) and can implement affine+nonlinear transforms with relatively few trainable parameters, suggesting potential suitability for near-term photonic NISQ devices.

#limitation:simulation-only — All experiments were run on simulators (Strawberry Fields TensorFlow backend and Qiskit statevector simulator); no physical QPU or noise model experiments were presented.

#limitation:no-empirical-validation — There is no real-hardware validation and important training/hardware-related hyperparameters (epoch counts, batch sizes, Fock cutoff) are not specified, limiting reproducibility and assessment under realistic noise.

#limitation:data-encoding — The approach relies on displacement-encoding into qumodes and required scaling/normalization to respect Fock-space truncation in simulation; the cost and fidelity of such encodings on hardware is not evaluated.
#limitation:qubit-count — Experiments use 4 qumodes (inputs) and small datasets (80-200 instances); scalability to larger feature sets, longer horizons, or larger markets is untested.

#quantum-linear-systems — The paper benchmarks a variational quantum linear solver (VQLS) as a discrete-variable baseline using Hadamard-test based costs; VQLS did not show superiority over CVQNN in these simulated experiments.
contradictions: The paper reports CVQNNs outperforming classical neural networks on some datasets (IBM, Yahoo examples) but shows classical or comparable performance on others (Energy dataset), so the claim of broadly superior performance is dataset-dependent and not uniformly supported.

The manuscript suggests near-term feasibility for CVQNNs (fewer parameters, natural continuous encoding) but provides only simulator-based evidence with unspecified Fock cutoffs and no noise/real-hardware experiments—this undermines claims about practical scalability and real-world deployment beyond the 4-qumode, small-dataset regime tested.
